newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ showing signs of losing the plot, says Matthew.
newsitem.headline: NZ showing signs of losing the plot, says Matthew.

text.p: New Zealand was showing signs of losing the plot and Australia was not much better, Business Roundtable vice-chairman Bob Matthew said in Sydney on Tuesday.

Matthew, who is also chairman of Brierley Investments and Air NZ, told the Australian Committee for Economic Development that economic and social reform in both countries was lagging behind more dynamic countries in Asia and elsewhere.
One of New Zealand's growth industries in recent years had been hosting Australian politicians, business leaders and industry association executives keen to study New Zealand's reforms, Matthew said.
"It is therefore with a sense of disappointment that I have to tell you New Zealand is showing signs of losing the plot."

New Zealand was drifting back to the "comfort zone" that led Labour prime minister David Lange to take a tea break in the 1980s and Prime Minister Jim Bolger to sack Ruth Richardson as Finance Minister after the 1993 election, Matthew said.
"So I caution any would-be Australian traveller to New Zealand not to expect a lot of inspiration from our recent record, or from our current agenda for further change."
Both Australians and New Zealanders were lagging behind other countries, he said.
Genuine political leadership of the type displayed by Roger Douglas and Richardson was, unfortunately, comparatively rare. Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett was another, Matthew said.
Neither country could afford to flag, but as a smaller and less robust economy, New Zealand would lose its attractiveness to investors without maintaining a margin of excellence over competitors.

Matthew said that as chairman of BIL and Air NZ he had a special interest in Australia's progress. BIL had $1.8 billion invested in Australia and about $1.6 billion invested in New Zealand. It was keenly aware of regulatory constraints in Australia including those affecting takeovers, aviation policy, media ownership and taxation, he said.
The Australian takeovers regime with its 20 percent threshold worked against shareholders' interests by protecting poor management and inhibiting industry reorganisation, he said.

New Zealand remained keen to develop the single aviation market and open skies policy that was the brainchild of Paul Keating's government in Australia. The Keating government later turned into a reluctant partner after Mr Keating intervened to raise the sale price of Qantas.
Continuing procrastination, Matthew said, was "geared to Qantas' interests rather than those of tourism or the travelling public".
BIL recently acquired a 19.9 percent stake in Australian newspaper group John Fairfax Holdings.
Matthew said Australia's restrictions on foreign media ownership sprang from a perception of the capacity of the various media outlets to shape collective views, values and culture, Matthew said.
New Zealand was at the forefront of the recognition that in an era of global communications networks that stance no longer had any validity.
Foreign investment in media did not lead to subversion of national culture, and Rupert Murdoch's Star TV was proving the opposite, he said.

Taxation rules in Australia and New Zealand biased choices between inward and outward investment and different forms of domestic investment, Matthew said. Both countries needed to develop a sound and comprehensive framework that recognised their economies were fully integrated into the global economy.
